sources.title: Reanalyzing the Wow! Signal - Foresight Institute

16K views · 383 reactions | Astronomer Jerry Ehman was just doing routine work on a quiet August night in 1977, reviewing stacks of perforated computer paper from Ohio State University's Big Ear radio telescope. But as his eyes scanned down the columns of letters and numbers, he stopped dead.

The telescope had picked up a continuous, incredibly powerful radio signal originating from the constellation Sagittarius. It wasn't just random cosmic noise. The signal was exactly 1420 megahertz—the precise frequency of hydrogen. For years, scientists had theorized that if an intelligent alien civilization wanted to say hello to the universe, they would broadcast on the hydrogen frequency because it's the most common element in the cosmos.

The transmission lasted exactly 72 seconds, rising in intensity as the telescope rotated into its path, and fading away perfectly as it rotated out. It was the exact mathematical signature of a point source in deep space. Stunned, Ehman grabbed a red pen, circled the vertical column of data (which read "6EQUJ5"), and scribbled a single word in the margin: "Wow!"

Despite decades of searching, using far more advanced equipment and pointing massive arrays at the exact same spot in the sky, astronomers have never heard it again. The 72-second broadcast remains the strongest candidate for an extraterrestrial radio transmission ever detected, leaving us to wonder if someone was simply passing by, or if Earth was just listening at the exact right moment.

excerpts.text:
| **At a Glance:** **[**The Wow! Signal**](/research/seti-101/the-wow-signal/ "The Wow Signal") (SETI 101 — SETI Institute)** * **What:** A strong, narrow-band radio signal (print-out sequence “6EQUJ5”) detected on Monday, August 15, 1977 by the Ohio State Radio Observatory (operated by Ohio State University) during a routine sky survey. * **Where:** The observatory’s 25-metre telescope in Ohio, scanning overhead skies in search of narrow-band signals. * **Key feature:** The signal rose and fell in a way consistent with the telescope beam sweeping across a fixed point in the sky — suggesting a celestial, rather than terrestrial, origin. * **Why it matters:** It remains the most famous single-event candidate for an intentional extraterrestrial transmission — or at least an unexplained signal — because despite numerous follow-ups, it has never been seen again. * **Current status:** Still unsolved — natural source, human interference, or something else? The mystery remains. * [https://www.seti.org/research/seti-101/the-wow-signal/](/research/seti-101/the-wow-signal/) |

It was late in the evening of Monday, August 15, 1977. The Ohio State Radio Telescope, a massive metal assemblage hunched across three acres of grassy farmland, was deep into its daily routine: observing the overhead skies in search of narrow-band signals.

But this day would not be like all the others in a SETI effort that would last 22 years. A signal, a strong signal, was detected – although no one would notice until the following morning. That’s when astronomer volunteer Jerry Ehman sat down to peruse the previous day’s observations.

excerpts.text:
Was it really a ping from an extraterrestrial society, a natural signal source, or simply terrestrial interference?

The answer is still unknown, largely because the signal has not been seen a second time. But despite the fact that in the 70s and 80s other strange, seen-only-once signals were logged by SETI experiments, the WOW signal remains the best known.

Robert Dixon, who was the director of the Ohio State Radio Observatory at the time of the WOW signal’s detection, says that the famous signal could very well be worthy of its celebrity status.

“The fact that the [signal] followed the telescope’s beam shape indicated it was at least as far away as the moon, and made it very unlikely to be any interfering signal,” notes Dixon. “Then it turned off when we observed that direction again immediately afterwards, indicating it was of intelligent origin, and not some natural phenomenon.”

“Efforts to re-observe it afterwards with other telescopes have been unsuccessful, so this will likely remain a perpetual mystery.”

excerpts.text: The Ohio State University Big Ear radio telescope detected in 1977 the Wow!

Signal, detected on August 15, 1977, by the Ohio State University’s Big Ear radio telescope, remains one of the most compelling potential instances of extraterrestrial communication (see e.g. [Wright 37](#bib.bib37) and references therein).

Ehman, exhibited a narrowband radio frequency of approximately 1420.456 MHz, which is notably close to the hydrogen line frequency, a region of the radio spectrum often considered a natural candidate for interstellar communication [[21](#bib.bib21)]. The signal lasted for 72 seconds, corresponding to the time it took the telescope beam to sweep past the source, but no follow-up observations have successfully replicated this anomaly [[16](#bib.bib16)].
